description: Todd V's flagship at-home drill: practice talking to a blank wall to desensitize yourself and groove the right frame before approaching real people. Level 1 -- talk to the wall for ~1 minute to get used to receiving NOTHING back (no nods, no validation) so silence stops rattling you. Level 2 -- talk to the wall while establishing the premise/intent, e.g. playfully tease it ('I like you, but you're so flat / so bland'). Level 3 -- talk to the wall from a high-value frame, speaking from the perspective that you are wanted, that the wall likes you, and that you're used to great social feedback. Progress through the levels over repeated sessions.

exercise_name: The 5-Phase Interaction Arc (Open / Premise / Evaluate / Narrative / Close)
description: Todd V's core conversation structure: run any man-to-woman interaction through five named phases so you always know where you are and what to do next. (1) OPEN -- only goal is to get the conversation going. (2) PREMISE / Intent -- establish early that you're evaluating her for a role in your life (man-assesses-woman frame). (3) EVALUATE -- judge her merit to justify continuing (hold the 'judge frame'). (4) NARRATIVE -- build the 'story of us two meeting', ideally framing the two of you together. (5) CLOSE -- via Pulling Dynamics: seed intentions and gauge interest, frame it as her win, qualify her, then lead with assumed compliance and a plan. Practiced by consciously labeling which phase you're in and rehearsing transitions.

Practice opening conversations using Todd's six categorized opener types and choosing the one that fits the situation and your skill level: super-direct (sexual), direct, direct-friendly (push-pull / observation), situational (tease / environment), opinion, and impersonal. Skill-graded guidance: beginners use direct openers to avoid 'coming across like friends'; intermediates balance direct and indirect; advanced practitioners use indirect openers carried by nonverbal undertones. Drill by writing/rehearsing one opener of each type and practicing delivering them.

A four-step routine for moving an interaction toward a close: (1) seed your intentions and gauge her interest, (2) frame the outcome as beneficial for her / her win, (3) qualify -- have her prove her worthiness / convince you, (4) lead with confidence and a predetermined plan, assuming compliance. Practiced as the 'Close' phase of the 5-phase arc; rehearse the seed-frame-qualify-lead sequence aloud.

Todd's tonality system: practice saying the same line in three vocal modes and feel how each changes your perceived status. (1) Seeking-rapport tonality -- voice rises like a question at the end (reads as lower-value, needing approval). (2) Neutral tonality -- flat, no inflection. (3) Breaking-rapport tonality -- voice falls at the end like a statement/command (reads as higher-value, authoritative). Drill: take one sentence and say it all three ways; aim to default to breaking-rapport. Pair with the right frame ('I have value / I'm the authority'), which produces authoritative tonality naturally.

Practice speaking with deliberate vocal range -- pitch moving up and down -- rather than a monotone. Todd's rule: if you tease with a monotone voice and a blank face you'll be rejected; the same words land as charming with expressive range and a smile. Drill by reading lines or telling a short anecdote while exaggerating pitch variation, pacing, and facial expression.

A formula for teasing that lands as playful rather than mean. Step 1 DELIVERY -- the only difference between a tease and an insult is delivery; smile, vary your tonality (up and down, not monotone), and deliver it like a joke expecting a good reaction. Step 2 SUBTLETY -- less is more; a short line ('Really? That's... kinda strange') beats a long witty one, because brevity creates uncertainty and invites her to invest; avoid over-gaming / revealing your agenda. Step 3 NEGATIVE ASSOCIATION ('by far the most important') -- instead of the default positive/agreeing response, find the negative or challenging angle (e.g. 'How can you possibly live in NYC, it's so busy you'd never sleep'). Built on negative polarity / reward-prediction-error. Practice by taking something she says and generating the subtle, smiling, negative-angle reply.

Practice flipping the frame so the other person earns your approval rather than the reverse. Techniques: ask whether you can trust her, tell her you're 'not sure' about her / 'not sure you can take her tonight' and let her convince you it's a good idea, or pre-define '5 things you want to see in her' and screen against them. The goal is to build her investment (investment -> attachment) while holding the judge frame. Caution against over-qualifying once she already likes you.

Core pedagogical exercise across The System and Verbal Game Academy: watch annotated real-life field footage (Todd's own interactions plus student infields, e.g. 'JP') with expert commentary analyzing conversation flow, frame management, phase transitions, and tactical adjustments, including student-infield clips that showcase beginner mistakes with advanced feedback. Practiced as guided observation -- pause and predict the next move, then compare to Todd's commentary -- and applied to one's own recorded/recalled interactions.

A mindset/state exercise: prioritize entertaining yourself in the interaction first, so your behavior reads as non-needy and outcome-independent. Approach conversations to amuse yourself rather than to win her approval; this self-amused frame underpins teasing, tonality, and frame control. Practiced as a pre-interaction reframe and a running internal check ('am I enjoying this, or performing for her?').

A drill for responding to a disinterested or screening target while keeping a high-value frame: (1) acknowledge her screening lightly ('Hey, it's okay, I'm [name]'), (2) maintain the high-value frame throughout (don't drop into supplication), (3) challenge her participation by teasing. Used to handle shit tests, last-minute resistance, and early disinterest without self-rejecting. Practiced by rehearsing calm, framed responses to common brush-offs.

A Week 0 'Fundamentals of Verbal Game' lesson teaching you to distinguish the conversational baseline (the ongoing vibe/banter you ride) from the plotline (narrative progression that pushes the interaction forward), and to choose when to stay in baseline vs. advance the plotline. A one-week conditioning drill (from Day Game by Todd): speak with decisive certainty for a week -- make clear 'yes/no' statements, give direct opinions, and remove hedging, qualifiers, and approval-seeking language from your speech. Builds an authoritative, high-value verbal frame.

A one-week frame-control drill (from Day Game by Todd): for a week, stop justifying or explaining yourself to others and stop seeking approval -- notice every urge to qualify yourself and don't act on it. Trains outcome-independence and a non-supplicating frame.

A one-week mindset-conditioning drill (from Day Game by Todd): for a week, deliberately hold only positive thoughts and reframe negatives, building the optimistic, abundant internal state that supports a confident outer game.

exercise_name: 10 Reasons You're the Best Thing That Can Happen to Her
description: A self-concept / value-frame writing exercise (from Day Game by Todd): write down 10 concrete reasons you would be the best thing to happen to her, to internalize a high-value, giving frame before approaching. Paired with '5 things you want to see in her' to pre-define your own qualification criteria so you screen rather than chase.

exercise_name: Talk to Groups in the Street (desensitization)
description: A field desensitization drill (from Day Game by Todd): approach and talk to groups of people in the street to normalize starting conversations and reduce approach anxiety, often combined with a minimum of three daily approaches and pre-deciding your goal type (number, short set, or instant date).
